claim: Arpin mRNA is expressed in different human and mouse endothelial cells.
source: We found here by end-point RT-PCR that arpin mRNA is expressed in different human and mouse endothelial cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Arpin protein is present in HMEC-1 and HUVEC at similar levels with the predicted molecular weight of 25 kDa.
source: Also, arpin protein is present in HMEC-1 (Human Microvascular Endothelial Cells) and HUVEC at similar levels with the predicted molecular weight of 25 kDa (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Arpin is localized throughout the cytosol in confluent HUVEC monolayers.
source: Arpin was localized throughout the cytosol in confluent HUVEC monolayers (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Line scans revealed an enrichment of arpin close to vascular endothelial cadherin (VE-cadherin) at cell-cell contacts.
source: However, line scans revealed an enrichment of arpin close to vascular endothelial cadherin (VE-cadherin) at cell-cell contacts. (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by line scan analysis of immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Arpin is localized throughout the endothelial cytosol with an enrichment near and at junctions in postcapillary venules of cremaster muscles.
source: Analyzing arpin localization in postcapillary venules of cremaster muscles using Platelet-Endothelial Cell Adhesion Molecule-1 (PECAM-1) as the template for endothelial cell-cell contacts, we observed a similar localization of arpin throughout the endothelial cytosol with an enrichment near and at junctions (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from mouse cremaster venules shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The enrichment of arpin at junctions observed both in human HUVEC culture and mouse cremaster venules suggests that arpin could contribute to endothelial barrier regulation.
source: Although the majority of arpin is localized in the cytosol, such enrichment at junctions observed both in human HUVEC culture and mouse cremaster venules suggests that arpin could contribute to endothelial barrier regulation.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed localization pattern of arpin at junctions.

claim: ARPIN gene expression is significantly downregulated by around 60% in HUVEC monolayers treated with TNFα for 4 and 18 hr.
source: To study arpin regulation during inflammation, we analyzed ARPIN gene expression by qRT-PCR in HUVEC monolayers treated with TNFα for 4 and 18 hr and found a significant downregulation of around 60% (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The expression of the other Arp2/3 inhibitors, AP1AR and PICK1, was not significantly changed after TNFα treatment.
source: Remarkably, the expression of the other Arp2/3 inhibitors, AP1AR and PICK1, was not significantly changed after TNFα treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Western blot and densitometry analysis confirmed the decrease of arpin at the protein level after TNFα treatment.
source: Western blot and densitometry analysis confirmed this decrease of arpin at the protein level (Figure 2B) with no significant changes in PICK1 protein levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There were no significant changes in PICK1 protein levels after TNFα treatment.
source: Western blot and densitometry analysis confirmed this decrease of arpin at the protein level (Figure 2B) with no significant changes in PICK1 protein levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Upregulation of Intercellular Adhesion Molecule-1 (ICAM-1) was used as a positive control for the inflammatory response.
source: Upregulation of Intercellular Adhesion Molecule-1 (ICAM-1) was used here as a positive control for the inflammatory response.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design using ICAM-1 as a control marker.

claim: Immunofluorescence of arpin in HUVEC monolayers treated with TNFα confirmed downregulation of arpin.
source: Immunofluorescence of arpin in HUVEC monolayers treated or not with TNFα confirmed downregulation of arpin (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Arpin was lost at junctions after TNFα treatment.
source: This decrease was not only obvious for total arpin, but arpin was also lost at junctions (arrows in the magnifications of Figure 2C) and actin filaments (Top-right graphs Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Arpin reduction significantly correlated with the TNFα-induced increase in actin stress fibers.
source: Interestingly, arpin reduction significantly correlated with the TNFα-induced increase in actin stress fibers (Below graph Figure 2C; Wójciak-Stothard et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2C and cited literature.

claim: Arpin protein downregulation was also observed after IL-1β treatment in HUVECs for 4 and 18 h.
source: Arpin protein downregulation was also observed after IL-1β treatment in HUVECs for 4 and 18 h (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and no significant changes were observed in the protein levels of PICK1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: No significant changes were observed in the protein levels of PICK1 after IL-1β treatment.
source: Arpin protein downregulation was also observed after IL-1β treatment in HUVECs for 4 and 18 h (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and no significant changes were observed in the protein levels of PICK1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: IL-1β induces loss of arpin at all subcellular locations.
source: Similar to TNFα-treatment, IL-1β induces loss of arpin at all subcellular locations (top-right graphs Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: IL1β-induced arpin downregulation significantly correlated with an increase in actin stress fibers.
source: Again, IL1β-induced arpin downregulation significantly correlated with an increase in actin stress fibers (lower graph Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Arpin immunofluorescence signal in post-capillary venules of the TNFα-inflamed cremaster muscle was reduced by around 50%.
source: Arpin immunofluorescence signal in post-capillary venules of the TNFα-inflamed cremaster muscle was also reduced by around 50%, which was again true for both junctional and non-junctional arpin (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from mouse cremaster venules shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Robust neutrophil recruitment confirmed that inflammation was induced correctly in the cremaster muscle model.
source: Robust neutrophil recruitment confirmed that inflammation was induced correctly in this model.
evidence: The claim is supported by neutrophil staining data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Endothelial arpin is downregulated in response to pro-inflammatory cytokines in vitro and in vivo.
source: Overall, endothelial arpin is downregulated in response to pro-inflammatory cytokines in vitro and in vivo suggesting that arpin plays an important role in the regulation of endothelial barrier dysfunction during inflammation.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental data from in vitro and in vivo models.

claim: Arpin plays an important role in the regulation of endothelial barrier dysfunction during inflammation.
source: Overall, endothelial arpin is downregulated in response to pro-inflammatory cytokines in vitro and in vivo suggesting that arpin plays an important role in the regulation of endothelial barrier dysfunction during inflammation.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed downregulation of arpin during inflammation.

claim: Arpin-depleted HUVEC showed more than 80% reduction in arpin protein levels.
source: To analyze the function of arpin in endothelial barrier regulation, we generated arpin-depleted HUVEC with more than 80% reduction in arpin protein levels (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Arpin depletion did not change the expression of arpC5, a subunit of the Arp2/3 complex, or the NPFs WAVE2 and WASP.
source: Of note, arpin depletion did not change the expression of arpC5, a subunit of the Arp2/3 complex, or the NPFs WAVE2 and WASP (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The paracellular flux of 150 kDa FITC-dextran across untreated arpin-depleted HUVEC monolayers was 34.5% (±3.70) higher.
source: Although arpin-depleted HUVEC formed monolayers, the paracellular flux of 150 kDa FITC-dextran across untreated arpin-depleted HUVEC monolayers was 34.5% (±3.70) higher (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by permeability assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: TNFα treatment of arpin-depleted HUVEC showed an even higher increase in permeability compared to control HUVEC treated with TNFα.
source: While TNFα treatment of control HUVEC induced the expected strong increase in permeability, TNFα treatment of arpin-depleted HUVEC showed an even higher increase compared to control HUVEC treated with TNFα (Figure 3B) suggesting that the TNFα-induced and arpin-induced permeability increases are regulated by different mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is supported by permeability assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The TNFα-induced and arpin-induced permeability increases are regulated by different mechanisms.
source: While TNFα treatment of control HUVEC induced the expected strong increase in permeability, TNFα treatment of arpin-depleted HUVEC showed an even higher increase compared to control HUVEC treated with TNFα (Figure 3B) suggesting that the TNFα-induced and arpin-induced permeability increases are regulated by different mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the additive effects of TNFα treatment and arpin depletion on permeability.

claim: No changes were observed in the total protein levels of the AJ proteins VE-Cadherin, β-catenin, and vinculin in control and arpin-depleted HUVEC.
source: However, we did not observe changes in the total protein levels of the AJ proteins VE-Cadherin, β-catenin, and vinculin in control and arpin-depleted HUVEC (Figure 3C), or in the levels of the TJ proteins ZO-1 and claudin-5 (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: No changes were observed in the levels of the TJ proteins ZO-1 and claudin-5 in control and arpin-depleted HUVEC.
source: However, we did not observe changes in the total protein levels of the AJ proteins VE-Cadherin, β-catenin, and vinculin in control and arpin-depleted HUVEC (Figure 3C), or in the levels of the TJ proteins ZO-1 and claudin-5 (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Immunofluorescence staining of VE-Cadherin and β-catenin revealed discontinuous and zipper-like junctional patterns, indicative of immature junctions in arpin-depleted HUVEC.
source: However, immunofluorescence staining of VE-Cadherin and β-catenin revealed discontinuous and zipper-like junctional patterns, indicative of immature junctions in arpin-depleted HUVEC (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The calcium switch assay showed that control and arpin-depleted HUVEC formed new junctions in a similar fashion.
source: Surprisingly, the calcium switch assay showed that control and arpin-depleted HUVEC formed new junctions in a similar fashion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium switch assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Arpin is not required for junction assembly, but rather for stabilizing existing junctions.
source: These data suggest that arpin is not required for junction assembly, but rather for stabilizing existing junctions.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the calcium switch assay results.

claim: A statistically significant increase in actin filaments was observed in arpin-deficient cells.
source: Quantifying the pixel intensity of the phalloidin stainings, we observed a statistically significant increase in actin filaments in the cells with arpin deficiency (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by phalloidin staining quantification shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Arpin-depleted HUVEC showed a significant increase in central actin filaments crossing the cell body.
source: Particularly, arpin-depleted HUVEC showed a significant increase in central actin filaments crossing the cell body (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by central actin fiber density quantification shown in Figure 4B.

claim: No significant differences were observed in the total actin protein levels in control and arpin-depleted HUVEC.
source: However, we did not observe significant differences in the total actin protein levels in control and arpin-depleted HUVEC (Figure 4C) suggesting that G-actin levels are reduced at the expense of F-actin formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: G-actin levels are reduced at the expense of F-actin formation in arpin-depleted HUVEC.
source: However, we did not observe significant differences in the total actin protein levels in control and arpin-depleted HUVEC (Figure 4C) suggesting that G-actin levels are reduced at the expense of F-actin formation.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation of increased F-actin without changes in total actin levels.

claim: Quantification of cortactin, coronin1B, and cofilin did not reveal any significant changes caused by the loss of arpin.
source: Quantification of other proteins known to be involved in actin dynamics such as cortactin, coronin1B, and cofilin did not reveal any significant changes caused by the loss of arpin (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Phalloidin stainings and quantification of the total F-actin signal revealed no reduction in the pixel intensity between CK666-treated and vehicle-treated arpin-depleted HUVEC.
source: Surprisingly, phalloidin stainings and quantification of the total F-actin signal revealed no reduction in the pixel intensity between CK666-treated and vehicle-treated arpin-depleted HUVEC (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by phalloidin staining data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The central actin fiber density was not affected by Arp2/3 inhibition in arpin-depleted HUVEC.
source: The central actin fiber density was also not affected by Arp2/3 inhibition in arpin-depleted HUVEC (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by central actin fiber density quantification shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Permeability increased in control HUVEC after CK666 treatment.
source: Interestingly, permeability increased in control HUVEC after CK666 treatment (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by permeability assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: CK666 induced an additional increase in permeability in arpin-depleted HUVEC instead of normalizing it.
source: Instead of normalizing the permeability in arpin-depleted HUVEC, CK666 induced an additional increase in permeability (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by permeability assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Arpin regulates actin filament formation and permeability in HUVEC in an Arp2/3-independent manner.
source: These surprising results demonstrate that arpin regulates actin filament formation and permeability in HUVEC in an Arp2/3-independent manner.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the lack of effect of Arp2/3 inhibition on arpin-depleted HUVEC phenotype.

claim: A significant increase in the phosphorylation of myosin light chain (MLC) at serine-19 was observed in arpin-depleted HUVECs, indicative of actomyosin contractility.
source: As shown in Figure 6A, we observed a significant increase in the phosphorylation of myosin light chain (MLC) at serine-19 in arpin-depleted HUVECs, indicative of actomyosin contractility.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: An increase in the phosphorylation of MYPT1 at Threonin-696 and Threonin-853 was found in arpin-depleted HUVECs.
source: Concomitant with the increase in p-MLC-S19, we found an increase in the phosphorylation of MYPT1 at Threonin-696 and Threonin-853 in arpin-depleted HUVECs (Figure 6B), phosphorylations known to inactivate MYPT1.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Phosphorylations at Threonin-696 and Threonin-853 are known to inactivate MYPT1.
source: Concomitant with the increase in p-MLC-S19, we found an increase in the phosphorylation of MYPT1 at Threonin-696 and Threonin-853 in arpin-depleted HUVECs (Figure 6B), phosphorylations known to inactivate MYPT1.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about MYPT1 regulation.

claim: Increased total levels of ROCK1 and ZIPK were observed in arpin-depleted HUVECs.
source: In agreement, we observed increased total levels of ROCK1 and ZIPK in arpin-depleted HUVECs that likely contribute to increased MLC phosphorylation (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Increased total levels of ROCK1 and ZIPK likely contribute to increased MLC phosphorylation.
source: In agreement, we observed increased total levels of ROCK1 and ZIPK in arpin-depleted HUVECs that likely contribute to increased MLC phosphorylation (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the known roles of ROCK1 and ZIPK in MLC phosphorylation.

claim: The levels of the formin mDia, implicated in the nucleation of actin stress fibers, were not affected by arpin depletion.
source: However, the levels of the formin mDia, implicated in the nucleation of actin stress fibers, were not affected by arpin depletion (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The increased central actin filaments in arpin-depleted HUVEC are contractile actomyosin stress fibers that contribute to the destabilization of endothelial junctions and increased permeability.
source: These results suggest that the increased central actin filaments in arpin-depleted HUVEC are contractile actomyosin stress fibers that contribute to the destabilization of endothelial junctions and increased permeability.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed increases in MLC phosphorylation and stress fiber formation.

claim: Y27632 treatment showed a reduction of the total levels of actin filaments in arpin-depleted HUVECs compared to vehicle-treated arpin-depleted HUVEC.
source: Phalloidin staining in arpin-depleted HUVECs treated with Y27632 (Figure 7A) showed indeed a reduction of the total levels of actin filaments (Figure 7B) and the central actin fiber density (Figure 7C) when compared to vehicle-treated arpin-depleted HUVEC.
evidence: The claim is supported by phalloidin staining data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: Y27632 treatment reduced central actin fiber density in arpin-depleted HUVECs compared to vehicle-treated arpin-depleted HUVEC.
source: Phalloidin staining in arpin-depleted HUVECs treated with Y27632 (Figure 7A) showed indeed a reduction of the total levels of actin filaments (Figure 7B) and the central actin fiber density (Figure 7C) when compared to vehicle-treated arpin-depleted HUVEC.
evidence: The claim is supported by central actin fiber density quantification shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The permeability in Y27632-treated arpin-depleted HUVEC was reduced to the levels of vehicle-treated control HUVEC.
source: While the permeability in Y27632-treated arpin-depleted HUVEC were reduced to the levels of vehicle-treated control HUVEC, they were still higher compared to Y27632-treated control HUVEC.
evidence: The claim is supported by permeability assay data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Arpin-depleted HUVECs treated with the ZIPK inhibitor HS38 showed total actin levels similar to control HUVEC treated with HS38 or vehicle.
source: Moreover, we observed that arpin-depleted HUVECs treated with the ZIPK inhibitor HS38 showed total actin levels (Figure 7E and F) and central actin fiber density (Figure 7G) similar to control HUVEC treated with HS38 or vehicle.
evidence: The claim is supported by phalloidin staining data shown in Figure 7E and F.

claim: Arpin-depleted HUVECs treated with the ZIPK inhibitor HS38 showed central actin fiber density similar to control HUVEC treated with HS38 or vehicle.
source: Moreover, we observed that arpin-depleted HUVECs treated with the ZIPK inhibitor HS38 showed total actin levels (Figure 7E and F) and central actin fiber density (Figure 7G) similar to control HUVEC treated with HS38 or vehicle.
evidence: The claim is supported by central actin fiber density quantification shown in Figure 7G.

claim: HS38 was not able to reduce actin filament formation in control HUVEC.
source: In contrast to Y27632, HS38 was not able to reduce actin filament formation in control HUVEC.
evidence: The claim is supported by phalloidin staining data shown in Figure 7E and F.

claim: Permeability assays showed a complete rescue in arpin-depleted HUVEC treated with HS38.
source: Permeability assays confirmed these data and showed a complete rescue in arpin-depleted HUVEC treated with HS38 (Figure 7H).
evidence: The claim is supported by permeability assay data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: The even higher permeability in TNFα-treated arpin-depleted HUVECs was reduced after HS38 treatment but not to the levels of control cells.
source: Of note, the even higher permeability in TNFα-treated arpin-depleted HUVECs was reduced after HS38 treatment but not to the levels of control cells indicating that ZIPK inhibition is able to rescue the permeability effect caused by the loss of arpin, but not the combined effect of TNFα treatment and loss of arpin (Figure 7I).
evidence: The claim is supported by permeability assay data shown in Figure 7I.

claim: ZIPK inhibition is able to rescue the permeability effect caused by the loss of arpin, but not the combined effect of TNFα treatment and loss of arpin.
source: Of note, the even higher permeability in TNFα-treated arpin-depleted HUVECs was reduced after HS38 treatment but not to the levels of control cells indicating that ZIPK inhibition is able to rescue the permeability effect caused by the loss of arpin, but not the combined effect of TNFα treatment and loss of arpin (Figure 7I).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the partial rescue of permeability by HS38 in TNFα-treated arpin-depleted cells.

claim: TNFα-induced permeability follows a different mechanism than the permeability effect caused by arpin depletion.
source: This result further suggests that TNFα-induced permeability follows a different mechanism than the permeability effect caused by arpin depletion.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the differential effects of HS38 on TNFα-induced versus arpin depletion-induced permeability.

claim: An arpin knockout mouse model was generated on the C57BL/6 genetic background using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome engineering targeting exon 3.
source: Finally, to unravel the role of arpin in vascular permeability, we generated an arpin knockout mouse model on the C57BL/6 genetic background using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome engineering targeting exon 3 with a pair of specific gRNA sequences (Figure 8A).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental method used to generate the knockout mice.

claim: PCR of genomic DNA samples extracted from the tails clearly distinguishes the three genotypes.
source: PCR of genomic DNA samples extracted from the tails clearly distinguishes the three genotypes (Figure 8B), and Western blot of arpin revealed its presence in different organs of wild-type mice, and its absence in knock-out mice (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by genotyping PCR data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Western blot of arpin revealed its presence in different organs of wild-type mice, and its absence in knock-out mice.
source: PCR of genomic DNA samples extracted from the tails clearly distinguishes the three genotypes (Figure 8B), and Western blot of arpin revealed its presence in different organs of wild-type mice, and its absence in knock-out mice (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Arpin-/- mice did not show any obvious phenotype and could not be distinguished from Arpin+/+ mice by visual inspection.
source: Arpin-/- mice did not show any obvious phenotype and could not be distinguished from Arpin+/+ mice by visual inspection.
evidence: The claim is based on observational data from the mouse colony.

claim: No changes were observed in development, appearance, weight, or susceptibility to diseases compared to Arpin+/+ mice in pathogen-free conditions.
source: We did not observe changes in development, appearance, weight (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), or susceptibility to diseases compared to Arpin+/+ mice in pathogen-free conditions.
evidence: The claim is based on observational and weight measurement data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Breeding female and male Arpin+/- mice generated offspring according to Mendelian ratios.
source: Breeding female and male Arpin+/- mice generated offspring according to Mendelian ratios (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by breeding data shown in Supplementary file 1a.

claim: Permeability in the lungs of Arpin-/- mice was around two-fold higher than in Arpin+/+ mice under basal conditions without any permeability-inducing stimulus.
source: Remarkably, permeability in the lungs of Arpin-/- mice was around two-fold higher than in Arpin+/+ mice under basal conditions without any permeability-inducing stimulus (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by lung permeability assay data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Vascular permeability was higher in Arpin-/- mice under basal conditions compared to Arpin+/+ mice in the back skin.
source: Also in the skin, vascular permeability was higher in Arpin-/- mice under basal conditions compared to Arpin+/+ mice (Figure 8E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Miles assay data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Histamine stimulation further induced permeability in Arpin-/- mice.
source: Of note, histamine stimulation further induced permeability in Arpin-/- mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by Miles assay data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Treatment with either the ROCK1/2 inhibitor Y27632 or the ZIPK inhibitor HS38 reverted permeability to the basal levels observed in Arpin+/+ mice.
source: Treatment with either the ROCK1/2 inhibitor Y27632 or the ZIPK inhibitor HS38 reverted permeability to the basal levels observed in Arpin+/+ mice, thus confirming our findings in arpin-depleted HUVEC.
evidence: The claim is supported by Miles assay data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Arp2/3 inhibition using CK-666 did not affect vascular permeability in the skin of Arpin-/- mice.
source: Interestingly, Arp2/3 inhibition using CK-666 did not affect vascular permeability in the skin of Arpin-/- mice (Figure 8E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Miles assay data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Arpin controls endothelial permeability via ROCK/ZIPK-dependent stress fiber formation and not via inhibition of the Arp2/3 complex.
source: Together, these results support the idea that arpin controls endothelial permeability via ROCK/ZIPK-dependent stress fiber formation and not via inhibition of the Arp2/3 complex.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the effects of ROCK/ZIPK inhibitors versus Arp2/3 inhibitor on permeability in Arpin-/- mice.

claim: No significant differences were observed in the protein levels of VE-Cadherin, β-catenin, vinculin, claudin-1 and –5, and tubulin in Arpin+/+ and Arpin-/- lungs.
source: Next, we analyzed by Western blot overall expression levels of different junction proteins but did not observe any significant differences in the protein levels of VE-Cadherin, β-catenin, vinculin, claudin-1 and –5, and tubulin in Arpin+/+ and Arpin-/- lungs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Histological analyses revealed normal lung histology in Arpin+/+ mice.
source: Histological analyses revealed normal lung histology in Arpin+/+ mice (Figure 8F, Images 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: The Arpin-/- lungs showed several abnormalities indicative of a vascular phenotype.
source: By contrast, the Arpin-/- lungs showed several abnormalities indicative of a vascular phenotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: The absence of arpin caused a reduction of the volume of the alveolar space.
source: For example, the absence of arpin caused a reduction of the volume of the alveolar space (Figure 8F, Image 3, asterisk), signs of hemorrhage and microhemorrhage (Figure 8F, Images 4 and 5, arrowheads), and the presence of interalveolar edema (Figure 8F, Image 6, asterisks).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: The absence of arpin caused signs of hemorrhage and microhemorrhage in the lungs.
source: For example, the absence of arpin caused a reduction of the volume of the alveolar space (Figure 8F, Image 3, asterisk), signs of hemorrhage and microhemorrhage (Figure 8F, Images 4 and 5, arrowheads), and the presence of interalveolar edema (Figure 8F, Image 6, asterisks).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: The absence of arpin caused the presence of interalveolar edema.
source: For example, the absence of arpin caused a reduction of the volume of the alveolar space (Figure 8F, Image 3, asterisk), signs of hemorrhage and microhemorrhage (Figure 8F, Images 4 and 5, arrowheads), and the presence of interalveolar edema (Figure 8F, Image 6, asterisks).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: The histological score was significantly increased in Arpin-/- mice.
source: Accordingly, the histological score was significantly increased in Arpin-/- mice (Figure 8F, graph below).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological scoring data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Lungs of Arpin-/- mice showed the presence of lymphocytes and macrophages.
source: Lungs of Arpin-/- mice also showed the presence of lymphocytes and macrophages.
evidence: The claim is based on histological observations.

claim: The number of leukocytes in the peripheral blood was not significantly altered in Arpin-/- mice compared with Arpin+/+ mice.
source: However, hemograms revealed that the number of leukocytes in the peripheral blood was not significantly altered in Arpin-/- mice compared with Arpin+/+ mice (Supplementary file 1b), indicating that the presence of lymphocytes and macrophages in the lungs of Arpin-/- mice is not simply due to an increased number of these cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by hemogram data shown in Supplementary file 1b.

claim: The presence of lymphocytes and macrophages in the lungs of Arpin-/- mice is not simply due to an increased number of these cells.
source: However, hemograms revealed that the number of leukocytes in the peripheral blood was not significantly altered in Arpin-/- mice compared with Arpin+/+ mice (Supplementary file 1b), indicating that the presence of lymphocytes and macrophages in the lungs of Arpin-/- mice is not simply due to an increased number of these cells.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the hemogram data.

claim: No differences were observed in total levels of PECAM-1 in Arpin+/+ and Arpin-/- lungs.
source: Although we did not observe differences in total levels of PECAM-1 in Arpin+/+ and Arpin-/- lungs, we observed a significant increase in the total levels of F-actin (Figure 8G, graph below), similar to what we observed in arpin-depleted HUVEC suggesting that the increased permeability in vivo is also due to an increase in the formation of actin stress fibers.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: A significant increase in the total levels of F-actin was observed in Arpin-/- lungs.
source: Although we did not observe differences in total levels of PECAM-1 in Arpin+/+ and Arpin-/- lungs, we observed a significant increase in the total levels of F-actin (Figure 8G, graph below), similar to what we observed in arpin-depleted HUVEC suggesting that the increased permeability in vivo is also due to an increase in the formation of actin stress fibers.
evidence: The claim is supported by phalloidin staining quantification shown in Figure 8G.

claim: The increased permeability in vivo is due to an increase in the formation of actin stress fibers.
source: Although we did not observe differences in total levels of PECAM-1 in Arpin+/+ and Arpin-/- lungs, we observed a significant increase in the total levels of F-actin (Figure 8G, graph below), similar to what we observed in arpin-depleted HUVEC suggesting that the increased permeability in vivo is also due to an increase in the formation of actin stress fibers.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the correlation between increased F-actin and permeability in both in vitro and in vivo models.
